en: The Questions of Milinda:
The Chapter on Inference, concerning the Question on Inference.
2. Questions on the Ascetic Practices (Dhutaṅga) “Behold the forest-dwelling bhikkhus,
who have plunged deep into the virtues of the ascetic practices.”
Again he saw a householder king established in the fruit of non-returning.
Having looked upon both of them, he—
A great doubt arose:
"If a householder could awaken to the Dhamma,
then the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) would be fruitless."
Crushing the arguments of opponents and skilled in the three Piṭakas—
come now, ask the best of speakers.
"He will dispel my doubt.
Then King Milinda approached the Venerable Nāgasena;
having approached and paid homage to the Venerable Nāgasena, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, King Milinda [addressed] the Venerable...
He said this to Nāgasena:
"Venerable Nāgasena, is there anyone who, being a householder living at home, enjoying sensual pleasures, dwelling in a bed crowded with children and wife,
using Kāsī sandalwood, wearing garlands, scents, and unguents, and accepting gold and silver..."
“Is there anyone adorned with a crest-jewel of variegated gems, pearls, and gold, by whom the peaceful, ultimate Nibbāna has been realized?

“No, Great King; it is not just one hundred, nor two hundred, nor three, four, or five hundred, nor a thousand, nor a hundred thousand, nor ten million, nor a hundred thousand million, nor a hundred thousand times ten million. Let that be aside, Great King.”
“There is realization for ten, for twenty, for a hundred, and for a thousand; by what method, then, shall I grant you the instruction?
“You yourself should explain this.
“In that case, Great King, I will speak to you by way of the hundred, the thousand, the hundred-thousand, or the ten-million.”

Or by the hundreds of millions, or the thousands of millions, or the hundreds of thousands of millions—whatever discourse there may be based on the conduct and practice of purification, and the qualities of the excellent dhuta-ascetic practices within the ninefold word of the Buddha, all of that will converge here.

Great King, it is just as when rain falls upon a region of ground with depressions, elevations, even and uneven places, and ridges; all that water flows away from there and converges into the great ocean, the sea.

In the same way, Great King, when there is an editor, whatever discourses exist within the ninefold word of the Buddha—whether they concern refined conduct, practice, the ascetic virtues (*dhutaṅga*), or the qualities of those who uphold them—all of these will converge here.

And herein, Great King, because of my clear intelligence, the elucidation of the underlying reasons will also converge; thus this meaning will be well-distinguished, manifold, complete, pure, and brought together.

"Just as, Great King, a skilled master scribe, when instructed and writing out a script, completes that script through his own proficiency, intelligence, and elucidation of the reasons, so that the script will be finished, complete, without deficiency;

even so, my own proficiency and intelligence shall converge here in the elucidation of the reasons, whereby this meaning will be well-distinguished, manifold, complete, pure, and properly brought together."

In the city of Sāvatthī, O Great King, there were about fifty million noble disciples—seventy-five thousand male lay followers (upāsakas) and three hundred thousand female lay followers (upāsikās)—who were established in the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala); all of them were householders, not those who had gone forth.

Furthermore, at that very same place, at the foot of the Kaṇḍamba tree during the Twin Miracle (yamakapāṭihāriya), twenty koṭis of beings attained realization; and again, during the instruction to Rāhula the Younger (Cūḷarāhulovāda).
In the Mahāmaṅgala Sutta, the Samacitta Pariyāya, the Parābhava Sutta, the Purābheda Sutta,
the Kalahavivāda Sutta, the Cūḷabyūha Sutta, the Mahābyūha Sutta, the Tuvaṭaka Sutta, and the Sāriputta Sutta,
there was a realization of the Dhamma by deities beyond the path of counting.
In the city of Rājagaha, there were three hundred and fifty thousand noble disciples, both laymen and laywomen, of the Blessed One;

furthermore, right there, during the taming of the elephant-king Dhanapāla, there were ninety crores of beings; at the assembly at the Pārāyana, at the Pāsāṇaka Cetiya, there were fourteen crores of beings;
again, in the Indasāla Cave, there were eighty crores of deities; and again, at Isipatana in Bārāṇasī—
In the first teaching of the Dhamma at the Deer Park, eighteen crores of Brahmās and immeasurable deities attained realization;
furthermore, during the Abhidhamma teaching on the Pandukambala stone in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, eighty crores of deities attained realization;
and at the Descent from the Gods, at the gate of Saṅkassa city during the miracle of the Opening of the World, thirty crores of humans and gods who were inspired attained realization.

Again, at Kapilavatthu among the Sakyans, in the Nigrodha Park, through the teaching on the lineage of the Buddhas and the teaching of the Mahāsamaya Sutta, there was a realization of the Dhamma by devatas beyond the path of calculation.

Again, at the assembly of the garland-maker Sumana; at the assembly of Garahadatta; at the assembly of the merchant Ānanda; at the assembly of Jambuka the Ājīvaka; at the assembly of the deva-son Maṇḍūka;
at the assembly of the deva-son Maṭṭhakuṇḍali; and at the assembly of Sulasā, the beauty of the city.
At the assembly at Sirimat-nagara-sobhini, at the assembly with the weaver’s daughter, at the assembly with Cūḷasubhaddā,
at the assembly with the brahmin of Sāketa to see the cremation ground, at the assembly at Sūnāparanta, at the assembly on the Sakka-questions,
and at the assembly on the Tirokuṭṭa and Ratana Suttas, there was, in each case, the realization of the Dhamma by eighty-four thousand beings; as far as—
Great King, while the Blessed One remained in the world, wherever he dwelt— in the three circles and the sixteen great provinces—
there, for the most part, two, three, four, five, a hundred, a thousand,
or a hundred thousand gods and humans realized the peaceful ultimate goal, Nibbāna.

“Those gods, O Great King, who were householders and not renunciants—these and many other hundreds of thousands of millions of deities, O Great King, being householders, living as laymen, and enjoying sensual pleasures, realized the true goal, Nibbāna.

“If, venerable Nāgasena, householders, living as laymen and enjoying sensual pleasures, realize the true goal, Nibbāna, then for what purpose do these ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) accomplish anything? For that reason, the ascetic practices would be performing no function.”
"Venerable Nāgasena, if diseases are pacified without mantras and medicines, what is the use of inducing vomiting, purging, and so forth, which only weaken the body?
If enemies can be subdued with the bare fists, what is the use of swords, spears, javelins, bows, arrows, clubs, and maces?
If one can climb a tree by grasping its knots, crooks, hollows, creepers, and branches, what is the use of searching for a long and sturdy ladder?"
If the equilibrium of the elements is attained by sleeping on the bare ground, what is the use of seeking out large, magnificent couches of pleasant touch?
If one is able to cross alone through uneven wildernesses that are full of danger and fear, what is the use of seeking out a great, well-equipped army?
If one is able to cross a river or lake with one's own arms, what is the use of seeking out permanent bridges or boats?
"If one is able to provide food and clothing for oneself, what is the use of attending upon others, engaging in pleasant conversation, or running after them?
If one finds water in a natural pond that has not been dug, what is the use of digging wells, ponds, or lotus-pools?

Even so, venerable Nāgasena, if householders living as laymen and enjoying sensual pleasures can realize the true, ultimate goal of Nibbāna, what is the use of undertaking the excellent ascetic qualities (dhutaguṇa)?"

“Furthermore, Great King, there are these twenty-eight qualities of the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*), which are qualities according to reality, by virtue of which the ascetic practices are cherished and aspired to by all Buddhas.
What are the twenty-eight?
Here, Great King, the ascetic practice is a pure livelihood, having happiness as its fruit, blameless, not causing suffering to others, and free from fear.”
It is non-oppressive, leading exclusively to growth, non-declining, free from deceit, protective, granting what is desired, a taming of all beings,
endowed with restraint, appropriate, independent, liberated, the destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, the destruction of delusion,
the abandoning of conceit, the cutting off of evil thoughts, the crossing beyond doubt, and the shattering of indolence; it is the abandoning of discontent.
Forgiveness that is incomparable and immeasurable, leading to the destruction of all suffering— these, O Great King,
are the twenty-eight qualities of the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), which are qualities according to reality, and by virtue of which the ascetic practices are cherished and aspired to by all Buddhas.
Those, O Great King, who properly cultivate these qualities of asceticism become endowed with eighteen qualities.
By which eighteen?
Their conduct is thoroughly purified; their practice is well fulfilled; their bodily and verbal actions are well guarded;
their mental conduct is thoroughly purified; their energy is well sustained; and fear is stilled.
One is free from the view of a self; resentment has ceased; loving-kindness is established; nutriment is fully understood;
one holds all beings in high esteem; one knows moderation in food; one is devoted to wakefulness; one is homeless;
one dwells wherever there is comfort; one is loathsome toward evil; and one delights in seclusion.
He is constantly diligent. Great King, those who properly cultivate the ascetic qualities (dhutaguṇa) become endowed with these eighteen qualities.
Great King, there are these ten types of persons worthy of the ascetic qualities.
Which ten?

He is faithful, possessed of shame, possessed of fortitude, free from deceit, discerning of meaning, not lustful, desirous of training, firm in his undertakings, abundant in non-remorse, and dwelling in loving-kindness. These, O Great King, are the ten persons worthy of the ascetic qualities (*dhutaguṇa*).
Those, O Great King, who are householders, living as laymen, enjoying sensual pleasures, yet who realize the peaceful, ultimate goal of Nibbāna—[they too are such persons].
All of them, in their previous births, had performed the preliminary service and prepared the ground for the thirteen ascetic practices (*dhutaguṇa*).
Having purified both their conduct and practice therein, even while remaining as householders today, they realize the peaceful, ultimate goal of *nibbāna*.

Great King, it is just as when a skilled archer first has his pupils in the practice hall perform the various stages: the handling of the bow, the taking up of the arrow, the gripping of the bow, the pressing of the fist, the bending of the fingers, the positioning of the feet, the grasping of the string, the bracing, the drawing back, the holding steady, the aiming at the target, and the release.
Having trained in shooting at targets made of straw, men, bundles of grass, chaff, heaps of clay, wooden boards, and lacquer,
and having gained favor in the presence of a king, one receives excellent gifts such as thoroughbred chariots, elephants, horses, wealth, grain, gold, silver, female and male slaves,
wives, and choice villages; even so, Great King, those householders living at home, enjoying sensual pleasures, [who seek] the true, ultimate Nibbāna—
They realize it; all of them, having cultivated the thirteen ascetic qualities (*dhutaguṇa*) and performed the preliminary work in previous births,
purified both their conduct and practice right there, and thus even while remaining as householders today, they realize the peaceful, ultimate goal of Nibbāna.
“Great King, it is not without prior practice in the ascetic qualities (dhutaguṇa) that the realization of arahantship occurs in a single lifetime alone;
rather, through supreme energy, supreme practice, and such a teacher and spiritual friend,
the realization of arahantship occurs.”
Or again, great king, just as a physician, a surgeon, having gratified his teacher with wealth or by fulfilling his duties,

and having learned the practice of grasping the knife, cutting, scraping, piercing, extracting the barb, washing the wound, drying it, applying medicinal ointments, inducing vomiting, purging, and administering enemas— having completed his training in the sciences,
performed his apprenticeship, and become skilled in hand— approaches a patient for the purpose of healing.
In the same way, Great King, those householders living as laymen who enjoy sensual pleasures yet realize the peaceful, ultimate goal of Nibbāna— all of them have, in previous births,
performed the preliminary service and prepared the ground for the thirteen ascetic qualities (dhutaguṇa).
Having purified both their conduct and practice right there, they now, while remaining merely householders, realize the peaceful, ultimate goal.
They realize Nibbāna, Great King; for those who are not purified by the ascetic qualities (dhutaguṇa), there is no breakthrough to the Dhamma.
Just as, Great King, seeds do not sprout without the pouring of water, even so, Great King, for those who are not purified by the ascetic qualities, there is no breakthrough to the Dhamma.
Or again, Great King, just as those who have not performed wholesome deeds and have not done what is noble do not go to a happy destination,
even so, Great King, for those who are not purified by the ascetic qualities (dhutaguṇa), there is no realization of the Dhamma. Great King,
the ascetic qualities are like the earth, in the sense that they are a foundation for those who desire purification.
“Great king, the ascetic qualities are like water for those desiring purity, in the sense that they wash away the stains of all defilements.
Great king, the ascetic qualities are like fire for those desiring purity, in the sense that they burn up the forest of all defilements.
Great king, the ascetic qualities are like wind for those desiring purity, in the sense that they blow away the dust and dirt of all defilements.”
“Great King, the ascetic qualities are like an antidote for those desiring purity, in the sense that they allay the disease of all defilements.
Great King, the ascetic qualities are like the Deathless for those desiring purity, in the sense that they destroy the poison of all defilements.
Great King, the ascetic qualities are like a field for those desiring purity, in the sense that they cause the crops of all the qualities of recluseship to grow.”
“Great King, the ascetic qualities are like a heart-captivating jewel for those desiring purity, in the sense that they grant all desired perfections as a boon.
Great King, the ascetic qualities are like a ship for those desiring purity, in the sense that they carry one across the great ocean of saṃsāra.
Great King, the ascetic qualities are like a refuge for the fearful for those desiring purity who are afraid of aging and death, in the sense that they provide consolation.”
"Great King, the ascetic qualities (dhutaguṇa) are like a mother to those desiring purity who are oppressed by the suffering of the defilements, in the sense that they provide assistance.

Great King, the ascetic qualities are like a father to those desiring purity who wish to increase their wholesome states, in the sense that they give birth to all the qualities of the ascetic life (sāmañña).
Great King, the ascetic qualities are like a friend to those desiring purity, in the sense that they do not deceive them in their search for all the qualities of the ascetic life."
“Great King, the quality of asceticism (dhutaguṇa) is like a lotus for those desiring purity, in the sense that it is unsullied by the stains of all defilements.
Great King, the quality of asceticism is like the finest fourfold incense for those desiring purity, in the sense that it dispels the foul odors of the defilements.
Great King, the quality of asceticism is like the king of mountains for those desiring purity, in the sense that it is unshakable by the winds of the eight worldly conditions.”
“Great king, the ascetic qualities are like space for those desiring purification, in the sense that they are everywhere free from grasping, and are vast, wide, extensive, and great.
Great king, the ascetic qualities are like a river for those desiring purification, in the sense that they carry away the stains of the defilements.

Great king, the ascetic qualities are like a good country for those desiring purification, in the sense that they provide a means of crossing over the wilderness of birth and the forest-thicket of the defilements.”

“Great King, the ascetic qualities (dhutaguṇa) are like a great caravan leader, in the sense that they bring those desiring purification to the city of Nibbāna—the supreme, excellent, secure, and fearless state which is empty of all fears.
Great King, the ascetic qualities are like a well-polished, stainless mirror, in the sense that they allow those desiring purification to see the true nature of conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra).
Great King, the ascetic qualities are like a shield, in the sense that they ward off the blows of the clubs of the defilements for those desiring purification.”
The ascetic qualities, great king, are like a parasol in the sense that they ward off the rain of the defilements and the scorching heat of the fires of passion for those who desire purity.
They are like the moon, great king, in the sense that they are longed for and desired by those who desire purity.
They are like the sun, great king, in the sense that they dispel the darkness and gloom of delusion for those who desire purity.

“Great King, the ascetic qualities (dhutaguṇa) are like the ocean for those desiring purity, in the sense that they are the source of the many kinds of excellent jewels of the qualities of recluseship, and in the sense that they are immeasurable, incalculable, and unfathomable.
Thus, Great King, the ascetic qualities are of great benefit to those desiring purity;
they dispel all distress and fever, dispel discontent, dispel fear, dispel existence, dispel rigidity, dispel defilement, dispel sorrow, dispel suffering, and dispel lust.”

It dispels hatred, dispels delusion, dispels conceit, dispels views, and dispels all unwholesome states; it brings renown, brings welfare, brings happiness, produces comfort, produces joy, and provides security from bondage;
it is blameless, with desirable and pleasant results; it is a mass of virtues, a heap of virtues, possessing immeasurable, incalculable, and measureless qualities—excellent, sublime, and supreme.
Just as, great king, people resort to food for the sake of support, to medicine for the sake of benefit, to a friend for the sake of assistance,
to a boat for the sake of crossing over, to garlands and perfumes for the sake of fragrance,
to a refuge for the fearful for the sake of fearlessness, and to the earth for the sake of a foundation; so too...

They attend upon others: they attend upon a teacher for the sake of a craft, they attend upon a king for the sake of fame, and they attend upon a precious gem for the sake of its power to grant desires.
In the same way, Great King, the noble ones attend upon the ascetic qualities for the sake of their power to grant all the virtues of recluseship.
Or again, Great King, just as water is for the sprouting of seeds, fire for burning, food for the maintenance of strength,
a creeper for binding, a sword for cutting, drinking water for the quenching of thirst, a treasure for providing relief, a boat for reaching the shore,
medicine for the allaying of disease, a vehicle for traveling in comfort, and a refuge for the fearful; [so too is this Dhamma].
A shield for dispelling fear; a king for the sake of protection; a shield, staff, clod of earth, club, and arrow for warding off enemies;
a teacher for instruction; a mother for nourishment; a mirror for looking; an ornament for beauty;
clothing for concealment; a ladder for ascending; a scale for removing inequality; and a mantra for recitation.
A weapon is for warding off those who would attack; a lamp is for dispelling darkness; wind is for extinguishing feverish heat;
a craft is for producing a livelihood; medicine is for protecting life; a mine is for producing gems; a gem is for adornment;
authority is for ensuring non-transgression; sovereignty is for exercising power.

In the same way, Great King, the ascetic qualities (dhutaguṇa) are for the growth of the seed of the ascetic life, for the burning away of the stains of the defilements, for the acquisition of the power of supernormal success (iddhi),

for the binding of the restraint of mindfulness, for the complete cutting off of perplexity and doubt, for the removal of the thirst and craving of desire, for providing the consolation of clear realization (abhisamaya),

for crossing over the four floods, for the pacification of the diseases of the defilements, for the attainment of the bliss of Nibbāna, and for the dispelling of birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.

For the protection of the qualities of the ascetic life; for the warding off of discontent and evil thoughts; for the instruction in the entire purpose of the ascetic life; for the nourishment of all the qualities of the ascetic life;
for the vision of serenity, insight, the paths, the fruits, and Nibbāna; for the performance of that which is most highly praised and extolled by the whole world and is exceedingly beautiful;
for the burning away of all states of woe; for the ascending to the summit of the mountain peak of the purpose of the ascetic life; and for the dispelling of the crooked, curved, and uneven mind.

It is for the purpose of performing excellent recitation regarding the teachings that are to be practiced and those not to be practiced; for the rebuking of all defilements, which are like enemies; for the dispelling of the darkness of ignorance;
for the extinguishing of the feverish heat of the threefold fire; for the production of subtle, delicate, and peaceful meditative attainments; for the protection of all the qualities of asceticism;

for the arising of the precious jewel of the factors of enlightenment; for the adornment of those who practice yoga; and for the non-transgression of blameless, skillful, subtle, and peaceful happiness.
For the sake of mastery over the entire noble dhamma common to all [arahants].
Thus, Great King, for the attainment of these qualities— namely, each individual ascetic virtue (dhutaguṇa)— in this way, Great King, the ascetic virtue is incomparable,
immeasurable, peerless, matchless, without equal, unsurpassed, and supreme.
It is best, distinguished, superior, extensive, broad, expansive, wide, heavy,
burdensome, and great. Now, Great King, if a person who has evil desires, is overcome by longing, is a deceiver, greedy, crafty, desirous of gain, desirous of fame,
desirous of reputation— being unfit, unattained, unworthy, undeserving, and inappropriate— who undertakes the ascetic practice (dhutaṅga), he...
He incurs double the punishment; he incurs the destruction of all virtues;
and in this very life, he receives contempt, mockery, reproach, derision, reviling, exclusion from communal meals, expulsion, ejection, banishment, and dismissal;
and in the future life, he will be cast into the great Avīci hell, which extends for a hundred yojanas and is filled with heat, boiling, intense heat, and a forest of flaming sparks.
For many hundreds of thousands of millions of years, he is cooked, turning over and over like a mass of foam, above, below, and across;
then, having been released from that, his limbs and members become emaciated, rough, and blackened; his head becomes shriveled, swollen, and hollow;
he is hungry and thirsty, possessing a hideous and terrifying form and appearance, with broken ears and nostrils, and eyes that are either wide open or closed; his limbs are diseased and putrid.
With his entire body covered in worms, like a mass of fire burning in a windbreak,
burning and blazing within, without protection or refuge, wailing with piteous cries of lamentation, parched with thirst,
and having become a great ghost-monk (samaṇa-mahāpeta), he wanders upon the earth uttering cries of distress.
Just as, Great King, if someone who is unfit, unworthy, unqualified, undeserving, and unsuitable— a lowly man of base birth—
were to be consecrated with the kṣatriya coronation, he would suffer the cutting off of his hands, the cutting off of his feet, the cutting off of both hands and feet,
the cutting off of his ears, the cutting off of his nose, the cutting off of both ears and nose, or the *bilaṅgathālikā* punishment, the *saṅkhamuṇḍikā* punishment, or the *rāhumukha* punishment.
He undergoes various kinds of tortures: being garlanded with fire, having his hands set ablaze, being wrapped in *eraka* grass, being clothed in rags from a dustheap,

being dressed in antelope skin, being baited with a hook and meat, being marked with coins, being scraped with salt and bark, being rolled over a crossbar, being crushed on a bed of straw, being doused with boiling oil, being devoured by dogs,
being impaled alive on a stake, having one's head cut off with a sword, and many other such forms of judicial punishment.
For what reason?
Because he was unfit, unattained, unsuitable, unworthy, improper, low-born, and of base lineage, yet he placed himself in a position of great sovereignty; he has overstepped his bounds.
In the same way, Great King, any person who is of evil desire... [and so forth].
He raises a cry of distress on the earth.
But as for that person, O Great King, who is disciplined, attained, worthy, fit, and suitable;
who is of few desires, contented, secluded, unassociated, energetic, resolute, not deceitful, not fraudulent, not gluttonous, not desiring gain, and not desiring fame—

One who desires no ill repute, who is endowed with faith and has gone forth out of faith, desiring to be liberated from aging and death, undertakes an ascetic practice (dhutaṅga) thinking, “I shall uphold the Dispensation.

Such a person deserves double the honor; he becomes dear, pleasing, beloved, and longed for by the devas, just as jasmine, jasmine-mallika, and other flowers are to one who has bathed and anointed himself, or like food to one who is hungry.
It is like exquisite food; like cool, pure, and fragrant water to one who is thirsty; like a supreme medicine to one afflicted by poison;
like a preeminent, excellent thoroughbred chariot to one desiring swift travel; like a captivating jewel to one seeking wealth;
like a bright, stainless white parasol to one wishing for consecration; and like the unsurpassed attainment of the fruit of Arhatship to one who loves the Dhamma.
For him, the four foundations of mindfulness reach full development;
the four right endeavors, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path reach full development.
He attains serenity and insight; his practice of realization comes to fruition; and the four fruits of recluseship [are attained].
The four analytical knowledges, the three true insights, the six direct knowledges, and the entirety of the ascetic’s duty—all these fall within his domain;
he is consecrated with the pure, stainless, and white parasol of liberation.
Great King, it is just as when a noble Kṣatriya king, born of a lineage of high birth, is consecrated with the royal Kṣatriya consecration.

The armies of his own kingdom, towns, and countryside attend upon him; the thirty-two royal assemblies, actors, dancers, bards, panegyrists, and the hosts of recluses, brahmins, and all the various sectarians approach him;
and whatever there is on earth—ports, jewels, mines, cities, customs stations, vassal states, and the administration of punishments and divisions among the people—he governs it all.
He becomes the master everywhere;
even so, Great King, whichever person is disciplined and has attained [the goal]...
[is consecrated] with the pure, stainless, white parasol of liberation.
There are, Great King, these thirteen ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), by means of which one who has purified himself enters the great ocean of Nibbāna and sports in the manifold play of the Dhamma;
he employs the eight attainments of the fine-material and immaterial realms, and he reaches the various powers, the divine ear-element, knowledge of others' minds,
recollection of past lives, the divine eye, and the destruction of all taints.

Which thirteen? The practice of wearing rag-robes, the practice of wearing the three robes, the practice of eating only by alms, the practice of begging for alms from house to house in regular order, the practice of eating at a single sitting, the practice of eating only from a single bowl,

the practice of not accepting food after having begun the meal, the practice of dwelling in the forest, the practice of dwelling at the foot of a tree, the practice of dwelling in the open air, and the practice of dwelling in a charnel ground.
The practice of sitting wherever one happens to be, and the practice of remaining in a seated posture— Great King, when these thirteen ascetic qualities have been practiced,
pursued, followed, cultivated, observed, performed, and fulfilled in the past,
one attains complete asceticism; and the entirely peaceful and blissful meditative attainments come under one's mastery.
Just as, great king, a well-provisioned shipmaster, having paid the proper customs at the port and entered the great ocean,
travels to Vaṅga, Takola, Cīna, Sovīra, Suratta, Alasanda, Kolapaṭṭana, Suvaṇṇabhūmi,
or to whatever other navigable sea-route there may be.
In the same way, Great King, when these thirteen ascetic qualities have been practiced,
cultivated, observed, fully observed, lived out, attended to, and fulfilled in the past, one attains the entirety of the state of a recluse;
the entire peaceful and blissful attainments come under one's mastery.

Just as, great king, a farmer first removes the defects of the field—grass, wood, and stones—and having ploughed, sown, properly watered, guarded, and protected it, becomes possessed of much grain through the harvesting and threshing, so that all those who are without wealth, miserable, poor, destitute, and wretched become his dependents; so too, great king, does a person of right view... [as before]... become a refuge for many beings. This is the fourth fruit of right view visible here and now, more excellent and sublime than the previous ones. Furthermore, great king, a person of right view, being endowed with right view, undertakes various wholesome deeds by way of body, speech, and mind. With the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world. There, having been born among the devas, he enjoys divine sensual pleasures.

Just as, great king, a merchant, having acquired a small amount of capital, engages in trade and, through successive transactions, becomes a possessor of great wealth, so that all those who are without wealth, miserable, poor, destitute, and wretched become his dependents; so too, great king, does a person of right view... [as before]... become a refuge for many beings. This is the fifth fruit of right view visible here and now, more excellent and sublime than the previous ones. Furthermore, great king, a person of right view, being endowed with right view, undertakes various wholesome deeds by way of body, speech, and mind. With the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world. There, having been born among the devas, he enjoys divine sensual pleasures. Just as, great king, a king’s frontier fortress is well-provisioned with grass, wood, water, and grain, and is well-guarded and protected against enemies and adversaries; and just as all those who are without wealth, miserable, poor, destitute, and wretched come to that royal frontier fortress seeking safety and protection; so too, great king, does a person of right view... [as before]... become a refuge for many beings. This is the sixth fruit of right view visible here and now, more excellent and sublime than the previous ones. (SN 45.2)
In the same way, Great King, when these thirteen ascetic qualities have been practiced in the past...
[omission] ...there arise the entirely peaceful and blissful attainments.

Or again, Great King, just as a consecrated Khattiya of noble birth is a master, a ruler, a lord, one who acts according to his will, possessing authority over the people to be punished or rewarded, and the entire great earth is under his control; so it is with these qualities.
In the same way, Great King, when these thirteen ascetic qualities (dhutaguṇa) have been practiced, pursued, observed, cultivated, performed, attended to,
and fulfilled in the past, one becomes a master, a wielder of power, a lord, and an agent of one's will within the sublime teaching of the Conqueror;
and all the qualities of a recluse come under one's control.
"Indeed, Great King, the Elder Upasena Vaṅgantaputta, out of his fulfillment of the ascetic qualities of effacement, disregarded the agreement made by the Saṅgha at Sāvatthī;

together with his retinue, he approached the Trainer of Men who had retired into seclusion, bowed his head at the Blessed One’s feet, and sat down to one side. And the Blessed One [addressed] that well-disciplined assembly..."
Having observed this, joyful, elated, glad, and uplifted, he conversed with the assembly and, with an unbroken Brahma-voice, said this:
“This assembly of yours, Upasena, is inspiring; how, Upasena, do you discipline the assembly?”
Questioned by the All-Knowing One, the Possessor of the Ten Powers, the God-Beyond-Gods, he spoke thus to the Blessed One according to his actual nature and qualities:

“Venerable sir, whoever approaches me and asks for the going-forth or for formal dependence, I say this to him: ‘Friend, I am a forest-dweller, an alms-food eater, a rag-robe wearer, and one who uses only three robes.
If you too will be a forest-dweller, an alms-food eater, a rag-robe wearer, and one who uses only three robes, then I will give you the going-forth.’”
“I will grant him dependence. “Venerable sir, if after promising me, he rejoices and desists, then I will let him go forth and grant him dependence;
but if he does not rejoice and does not desist, I will not let him go forth nor grant him dependence.
In this way, venerable sir, I shall discipline the assembly.”
In this way, Great King, one who has undertaken the excellent qualities of ascetic purification (dhutaguṇa) becomes a lord over the sublime teaching of the Conqueror.
He is a master, a sovereign, acting according to his will; all the peaceful attainments (samāpatti)—tranquil and entirely his own—become subject to him.
Just as, Great King, a lotus that has fully grown, pure, born of the sun, and produced from light, is glossy, soft, and desirable.
Fragrant, lovely, desired, and praised; unstained by water or mud; adorned with minute petals, filaments, and pericarps;
frequented by swarms of bees;

and nourished by cool water—just so, Great King, when these thirteen ascetic qualities (dhutaguṇa) have been practiced, pursued, followed, cultivated, performed, observed, and fulfilled in the past, the noble disciple becomes endowed with thirty excellent qualities.
What are these thirty excellent qualities?
He possesses a mind that is affectionate, gentle, soft, and full of loving-kindness; he has destroyed, struck down, and eliminated the defilements; he has slain and laid low pride and conceit;
he possesses unwavering, firm, well-established, and confident faith; and he is a recipient of the attainment of peaceful bliss, which is perfect, nourishing, exhilarating, and alluring.
He becomes one who is perfumed by the supreme, excellent, peerless, and pure fragrance of virtue; he is dear and pleasing to gods and humans;

he is longed for by the noble persons whose taints are exhausted; he is honored and worshipped by gods and humans; he is praised, extolled, lauded, and commended by wise, enlightened, and learned people;
he is unstained by the world, whether in this life or the next, even regarding minor faults.

Seeing fear, he is the accomplisher of the supreme goal of the paths and fruits for those desiring vast and excellent attainments; he is a recipient of abundant and exquisite requisites offered by others;

he is one who dwells without a home, devoted to the sublime dwelling of meditative absorption; he is the ground upon which the web of defilements has been disentangled; his hindrances to progress have been shattered, broken, crushed, and cut away;
he is of unshakable nature, a dweller in the forest, a consumer of blameless gains, liberated from the rounds of rebirth, having crossed over all doubt, and one whose purpose is fixed on liberation.

He has seen the Dhamma, has attained a firm refuge that is unshakable by fear, has severed the underlying tendencies, has reached the destruction of all taints, dwells frequently in the attainment of peaceful bliss, and is endowed with all the qualities of a recluse; thus he is possessed of these thirty supreme qualities.
Is it not so, Great King, that the Elder Sāriputta was the foremost person in the ten-thousandfold world system, setting aside the One Possessed of Ten Powers?
He too, the teacher of the world, having accumulated roots of merit over immeasurable and incalculable eons,
having renounced delightful sensual pleasures and many hundreds of excellent riches while born into a brahmin family, went forth in the teaching of the Conqueror; and having tamed his body, speech,
and mind with these thirteen ascetic qualities (dhutaguṇa), he is now, at this present time, endowed with infinite virtues as Gotama’s [disciple].
He has become one who sets in motion the Wheel of Dhamma in the supreme teaching of the Blessed One.
This was also spoken, Great King, by the Blessed One, the God above Gods, in the *Ekaṅguttaranikāya*:
“Monks, I do not see even a single person who can set in motion the unsurpassed…” [as the Tathāgata has done].
“He causes the Wheel of Dhamma that has been set in motion by the Tathāgata to turn correctly, even as it was turned;
for it is Sāriputta, monks, who causes the unsurpassed Wheel of Dhamma set in motion by the Tathāgata to turn correctly.

“Excellent, venerable Nāgasena! Whatever constitutes the ninefold word of the Buddha, whatever supramundane activity, and whatever abundant and noble attainments there are in the world—all of that is encompassed within the thirteen ascetic qualities (dhutaguṇa).”
